summary:
Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity under its penal code, and the applicable penalty is reported inconsistently across sources. The Human Dignity Trust country profile gives a maximum of three years' imprisonment. Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, cites Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as carrying six months to two years plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 Comorian francs (US$240 to 720). A Washington Blade report of 23 December 2024 cites Article 318 with a maximum of five years in the account of the December 2024 sentencing. Visitors should treat any same-sex intimacy, including private conduct between adults, as carrying a real risk of prosecution.

Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical. Outright International records a first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy in 2022 following a leaked video. In June 2024 two women were arrested after asking an imam to marry them, and on 12 December 2024 a Comorian court sentenced them to five and six months respectively for homosexuality before releasing them with the terms served. Reuters reported the release the same day. The Human Dignity Trust described the case as a human-rights violation, and it is reported as the first conviction of this kind.

The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report states that authorities recorded no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law in that year, and that no violence against LGBTQI+ persons was reported that year. That reporting period precedes the June 2024 arrests and the December 2024 conviction, so it does not describe the current enforcement picture. The same report lists widespread impunity among the country's major human-rights problems.

There is no law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Outright International reports that Comoros has no mechanism for legal change of gender marker. Documents presented at entry will therefore reflect the sex recorded at issuance, with no domestic route to amend them.
tangentialFactors:
Police reported that they do not incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and none was reported during 2023 according to the US State Department report. That statement is a single-year finding and sits alongside the same report's finding of widespread impunity in the justice system.

The government has repeatedly declined United Nations recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct, which indicates that the statutory position is a settled policy choice rather than an unenforced relic awaiting repeal.

The gap between reported penalties matters for anyone weighing risk: sources give three to five years as the outer range, while the only reported custodial sentences to date were five and six months served in full before release.

The 2010 US State Department Human Rights Report for Comoros contains only limited content on LGBT issues and is now dated; the more recent reporting is the 2023 country report and the 2024 press coverage of the prosecution.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory non-discrimination protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no legal procedure for changing gender marker on official documents.

Outright International reports that no LGBTIQ organisations are known to operate in Comoros, and that Article 5 of Law 86-006/AF deters registration of such bodies. Organised community support is therefore effectively unavailable domestically.

The December 2024 prosecution arose from a private request to an imam, indicating that conduct known to community or religious figures can reach the authorities even where routine enforcement appears low.

Widespread impunity in the wider justice system, as documented by the US State Department, conditions how any complaint by a resident is likely to be handled.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not agree on which penal code article governs or on the maximum penalty. Article 300 with six months to two years and a fine, a three-year maximum, and Article 318 with five years all appear in the inventory. The five- and six-month sentences actually imposed in December 2024 are recorded, but the article the court applied is not stated consistently.

Unresolved: the inventory does not say whether the two women convicted in December 2024 appealed, nor whether any further same-sex conduct prosecutions have been brought since that date.

Not sourced: there is no information in the inventory on screening of travellers for sexual orientation or gender identity at ports of entry, on detention conditions specific to LGBT detainees, or on the availability of legal gender recognition by any route other than the reported absence of a domestic procedure.

Not sourced: no data is available on hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions applying to offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity.
